column4: The source section names the root ن-ه-ر for harsh rebuke; 17:23 uses تَنْهَرْهُمَا to forbid scolding parents and replaces it with a gracious word, extending the ban on the hard verbal grip to the home.

The section contrasts قهر, lowering another person, with lowering one's own wing. Here the wing is lowered to parents out of mercy, and the verse asks for mercy in return for their raising the speaker as a child.

The section cites this exact case: when turning away from people whose request one cannot meet, give them قَوْلًا مَيْسُورًا, an easy word. It makes gentle speech the response even when provision is unavailable.
The section cites this contrast: قَوْلٌ مَعْرُوفٌ وَمَغْفِرَةٌ is better than charity followed by أَذًى. A gift loses its kindness when the giver adds injury.
The section cites the inheritance gathering where relatives, orphans, and the poor are to receive provision and قَوْلًا مَعْرُوفًا. Material giving and considerate speech meet in the same scene.

This covenant joins kindness to parents, relatives, orphans, and the needy with وَقُولُوا لِلنَّاسِ حُسْنًا. It places good speech beside care for the vulnerable, as the section joins the orphan and asker to gentle treatment.
The verse orders provision and clothing for dependants and قَوْلًا مَعْرُوفًا toward them. It makes the section's soft hand both material care and decent speech.
The section cites لِنتَ لَهُمْ as the Prophet's gentleness and says it is mercy; this verse contrasts it with a harsh, hard-hearted stance that would scatter people from around him.

The section cites the command to Moses and Aaron to address Pharaoh with قَوْلًا لَيِّنًا. Even this ruler is approached with a soft word, sharpening the contrast with the section's forbidden harsh speech.
The section explicitly reserves قهر for God's authority and contrasts it with Pharaoh's boast. This verse calls God الْقَاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبَادِهِ, grounding that boundary in divine power.

This repeats the section's divine-side formulation, الْقَاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبَادِهِ. Its context adds God's guardians over people, reinforcing the distinction between God's sovereignty and a human's abuse of the vulnerable.
The section cites Pharaoh's boast وَإِنَّا فَوْقَهُمْ قَاهِرُونَ as the human imitation of divine قهر. The verse supplies the tyrant's own claim of mastery over his people.

The source section's dictionary note for the root ق-ل-ي gives driving or herding as a secondary sense of 93:3. This verse forbids وَلَا تَطْرُدِ those who call on their Lord morning and evening, a direct reversal of driving people away.

After the prohibition on expelling the humble callers in 6:52 and the status question in 6:53, this verse tells the Prophet to greet believers with سَلَامٌ عَلَيْكُمْ and names mercy. It supplies the welcoming speech that answers exclusion.
The verse says وَاخْفِضْ جَنَاحَكَ to believers who follow the Prophet. It repeats the section's image of lowering one's own wing, the bodily opposite of forcing another down.
Alongside a warning not to strain one's eyes toward others' worldly gifts, this verse says to lower one's wing to believers. It joins the section's provision theme to humility toward people.

The story explains that the wall protected treasure belonging to two orphans until they matured, by mercy from their Lord. This is a concrete image of sheltering vulnerable children and guarding what is theirs, opposite to قهر.
This verse uses أَعْطَى, the same giving root named in the section, for one who gives and is mindful. It makes the section's yielding, generous hand an ethical act.
The ease promised after the giving in 92:5 is stated as فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرَى. It links the section's soft giving and its dictionary sense of ease in living to a path made easy.

The verse commands patience with those who call on their Lord morning and evening and forbids turning one's eyes from them for worldly adornment. It echoes 6:52's humble callers and opposes status-based exclusion.

This verse joins spending wealth on orphans, needy people, travelers, and السَّائِلِينَ to faith and care. The shared vulnerable recipients connect the section's gift and its refusal to rebuke the asker.

Continuing the charity passage around 2:263, this verse says spenders do not follow their giving with reminders or injury. Its own contribution is to keep a gift from turning into a verbal or emotional burden.
The next verse warns that reminders and injury can nullify charity. It completes 2:263's boundary: giving cannot justify the hard treatment the section forbids.

Following the ban on expelling callers in 6:52, this verse shows people questioning why the socially lowly received God's favor. It exposes status contempt as the pressure behind the exclusion the section rejects.

After 4:8's inheritance gathering and kind speech, this verse asks people who fear leaving weak offspring to speak قَوْلًا سَدِيدًا. It extends considerate speech to children exposed to vulnerability.

Asked about orphans, the verse answers that their improvement is best and calls them brothers. It gives a constructive relation to the orphan that counters the section's prohibition on overpowering him.
This command to do good includes parents, relatives, orphans, and the needy in one list. It supplies a positive counterpart to the section's specific bans on crushing and rebuking vulnerable people.
The verse gives the poor asker and deprived person a known share in the giving community's wealth. That standing makes the section's command not to rebuke the asker concrete.
The verse describes a known right in the wealth for people who ask and those deprived. It treats the asker as a rightful recipient, complementing the section's ban on answering him harshly.
This completes the preceding description by naming the recipients as السَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ. The asker in the section is thus part of a repeated Quranic scene of provision.
The righteous feed the needy, the orphan, and the captive despite their own love of the food. It turns the section's soft hand toward vulnerable recipients into a concrete act of care.
The next verse says they seek neither repayment nor thanks for feeding them. It completes the feeding scene with a giving stance free of leverage over its recipients.
The steep path includes feeding an orphan who is near of kin. This is a concrete caring act toward the very vulnerable figure whom the section says not to overpower.
The next act is feeding a needy person in the dust, bringing the section's treatment of the asker beside provision for someone in visible need.
After the feeding acts in 90:15–16, this verse names those who believe and counsel one another to compassion. It gives the care scene its communal quality.
The verse tells the Prophet's servants to say what is أَحْسَنُ, because Satan sows discord between them. It parallels the section's replacement of harsh rebuke with words that do not wound.
The instruction to invite with wisdom and good exhortation and to argue in the best manner makes measured speech an explicit religious stance, echoing the section's gentle word even to Pharaoh.
The verse commands دفع evil with what is better, saying that an enemy may become like a close friend. It gives a specific response to hostility opposite to answering with a harsh verbal grip.
This command also says to repel evil with what is best. In its own context it asks God to ward off the opponents' descriptions, extending the section's soft-response principle to hostile speech.
The Prophet is told to endure what people say and leave them with a graceful parting. That measured response contrasts with the harsh verbal grip named in the section.

This verse forbids turning one's cheek in contempt and walking on earth arrogantly. It supplies the proud bodily stance opposite to the section's calm, yielding walk and its refusal to put others down.

The following verse tells the listener to وَاقْصِدْ فِي مَشْيِكَ and lower the voice. Its measured gait and speech echo the section's dictionary note for ه-د-ي as calm walking and its contrast with harsh speech.
The servants of the Merciful walk humbly, and answer ignorant address with سَلَامًا. It joins the section's calm-walking sense to a non-harsh verbal response.
The verse orders orphans' property returned and forbids consuming it into one's own wealth. It makes material exploitation of an orphan a concrete form of the oppressive grip the section bans.
Guardians must return the orphans' property when they mature and not consume it hastily beforehand. The prohibition on rushing to take it contrasts with the section's unhurried, yielding posture.
Those who consume orphan property unjustly are described as swallowing fire. This starkly marks the material opposite of the section's command not to dominate an orphan.
The verse forbids approaching an orphan's property except in the best manner until maturity. It makes the section's prohibition on crushing an orphan apply to the handling of his property too.
This ruling calls for justice toward orphan girls whose prescribed rights are withheld. It specifies one way an orphan can be overpowered, extending the section's ban to unequal treatment.
The denier of judgment is described as يَدُعُّ الْيَتِيمَ, roughly thrusting the orphan away. This is a direct contrary action to the section's ban on overpowering him.
The next verse condemns failing to urge feeding the poor. It completes the orphan's rejection with neglect of provision, against the section's gentle treatment and giving image.
The passage condemns failing to honor the orphan. This directly reverses the respect and shelter implied by the section's account of finding the Prophet an orphan and providing for him.
The next failure is not urging the feeding of the poor. It places provision for the needy beside the section's gift and its restraint toward the asker.
The passage then condemns devouring inheritance greedily. This supplies a material form of the hard grip against the vulnerable that the section forbids.
This is the opposing branch to 92:5: the person who withholds and sees himself as self-sufficient receives the hard way, reversing the section's image of soft, yielding giving.
After the withholding and denial described in 92:8–9, this verse says the hard way will be made easy for that person. It completes the contrast to 92:5–7's giving and eased path.
In prison, Joseph contrasts many lords with اللَّهُ الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ. The same root named in the section locates ultimate mastery in God rather than in human dominators.
This verse calls God الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ while contrasting the Creator with powerless partners. It reinforces the section's distinction between divine قهر and human oppression.
On the Day the earth is changed, the verse names God الْوَاحِدِ الْقَهَّارِ. It places the root's absolute force in God's domain, the boundary the section draws against tyrannical humans.
The declaration that there is no god but Allah الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ repeats the root in the section's divine-authority contrast.
Rejecting the claim that God takes a child, this verse names Him الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ. Its context again makes the section's root belong to God's unique sovereignty.
At the gathering when the hidden is exposed, the verse says dominion belongs to Allah الْوَاحِدِ الْقَهَّارِ. It anchors the section's contrast between God's power and a human's domination.

The opening describes a man who عَبَسَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ when a blind person came. Though the visitor is a seeker rather than clearly the material petitioner of 93:10, the scene warns against a brusque response to someone approaching in need.
The next verse identifies the visitor as the blind man. This completes the encounter behind the frown and turn in 80:1, a concrete counterpart to the section's concern for a vulnerable asker.

The passage later describes another person who جَاءَكَ يَسْعَىٰ, coming to the Prophet with effort. It brings a seeker into the same scene of attention and neglect that illuminates the section's treatment of the asker.
This seeker is described as one who fears, giving a reason to attend to him rather than overlook him. It echoes the section's refusal to dismiss a supplicant harshly.
The passage says the Prophet is distracted from that seeker. This completes the warning in 80:1–2 about turning away, a neglectful boundary related to the section's prohibition on rebuking the asker.

The needy described here avoid persistent asking, so they are easy to overlook; this is not the same as the section's explicit petitioner, but it plausibly widens its concern to a less audible form of need.

The section's dictionary note for the root ض-ح-و says it carries the sense of not hurrying; 79:29 brings out the earth's ضُحَاهَا after darkening its night, repeating the dawn-and-night scene behind the section's opening.
The section explicitly glosses the root س-ج-و as stillness and applies it to night. This verse calls night سَكَنًا, a settled time, while placing sun and moon in measured courses.
The section's gloss of night as stillness is made explicit here: God made night لِتَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ, for people to rest in it, and day for seeing.
This verse likewise says night was made لِيَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ and day made bright for sight. It repeats the settled-night scene that the section draws from 93:2.
The verse calls night a time لِتَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ and day a time of sight, then names this as God's favor. It gives another direct formulation of the section's still-night image.
The verse makes night a covering, sleep a rest, and day a time of rising/spreading. It expands the section's quiet-night and dawn pairing into the body's rest and return to activity.
The verse names night as a time for rest and day as a time to seek God's bounty. It joins the section's settled night with its soft-giving and ease-in-living details.

The section's root ء-و-ي includes tenderness toward someone; Joseph here takes his brother إِلَيْهِ and tells him not to grieve over what the others did. The sheltering gesture makes that tenderness concrete.

The youths take refuge in the cave, أَوَى الْفِتْيَةُ إِلَى الْكَهْفِ, and ask God for mercy and right guidance. It repeats the section's sheltering-a-vulnerable-person image through the same refuge root it discusses.

The youths are told to take refuge in the cave, فَأْوُوا إِلَى الْكَهْفِ, where their Lord will spread mercy and ease their affair. This gives the shelter image an explicit movement from protection to mercy.

The section's dictionary note for ق-ل-ي includes driving a flock away. Noah says وَمَا أَنَا بِطَارِدِ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا when elite listeners want the believers gone, directly reversing that expulsive action.

Noah repeats that he is not one to drive believers away. In its own exchange, this verse rejects the social exclusion the section's secondary flock-driving sense and its ban on hard treatment illuminate.

The verse describes oppressed men, women, and children calling for rescue from a town of wrongdoers. Their subjection gives a concrete human scene for the section's account of قهر as domination joined to humiliation.

The verse forbids approaching an orphan's property except in the best manner until maturity and commands fair measure. It extends the section's ban on overpowering an orphan to safeguarding his material rights.
After Noah refuses to drive believers away in 11:29, he asks who could protect him from God if he did so. This verse contributes the accountability behind that refusal.

The leaders call Noah's followers “the lowliest” just before Noah refuses to drive believers away in 26:114. This verse supplies the status contempt that presses against the section's command not to put down the vulnerable.

The section's dictionary note for ع-ط-و describes an obedient, nonresisting camel and a pliant bow. This verse describes mounts made subservient and asks riders to remember God's favor when they settle on them.

The two women hold their flock back until the shepherds leave and explain that their father is old. This specific vulnerable-flock scene connects to the section's secondary account of driving a herd and its concern for a gentle response to someone in need.
After the women's explanation in 28:23, this verse says Moses watered for them and then withdrew to shade. Its own contribution is practical help for people whose need he has just heard.

The instruction is to argue with the People of the Book in the best manner, except those who act unjustly. It gives another explicit boundary for measured speech alongside the section's soft word to Pharaoh and its ban on rebuking the asker.
The verse forbids walking on earth with arrogance. This is a specific contrary gait to the section's dictionary gloss of ه-د-ي as calm, well-conducted walking.
For retaliation, the verse permits only equal measure and says patience is better. It sets a limit on the overpowering response that the section's account of قهر warns against.

The verse bounds retaliation for an injury by equivalence, then commends pardon and reconciliation. It clarifies the difference between just redress and the domineering, humiliating grip the section prohibits.

The verse warns the Prophet's wives not to soften their speech in a way that invites desire from a sick-hearted listener, while commanding an appropriate word. This is a contextual boundary on the section's soft-speech image, which is directed toward the vulnerable and even toward Pharaoh.
